questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had already been to Japan before, so I knew what the country was like. But the aspects were probably affordability, great food, interesting culture and a big city to explore.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
UTokyo gets 9/10 for me, with one point reducted due to problems with course selection and lack of social aspects at orientation.
I studied at the graduate school of economics, so if someone reads this, everything related to the school will be different for other graduate schools / undergraduate.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I would say that overall, the information is quite easy to find, but there is a lot of information to keep track of. Most of the difficult stuff is pre-arrival. Once you arrive its relatively simple, and you get an entire book with information that you can look through.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Before I arrived, I was assigned a tutor. My tutor helped me signing up for several things at the local municipal office like health insirance and other stuff. I think this proccess would be quite overwhelming without someone speaking Japanese, so that was nice. Second, we had an orientation. Here we got needed information, and I wasnt really unsure of anything. 40% of it was in Japanese because some people were not comfortable speaking English, but that was also a little fun to experience so not really a problem. The only thing that could have been done much better was some sort of social activity, or just a chance to meet people. I naturally met the only 3 other non-asian people out of 50 attendees, because we knew we could speak English, but there wasnt really any chance to meet the other economics students which I thought was a shame. 2 of them became my closest friends, but without the orientation I would probably have had less of a social experience

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: One point reduced because of no social activities. I know that the under-grad program had some meet and greet stuff. I have also studied in the US where there were several events extending the orientation.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Two best options are Komaba or Mejirodai. I was in Komaba Main which is probably the best of all options, with Komaba Annex probably being just as good. Komaba B-C is cheaper but has shared toilets/baths, which I wouldnt like myself. I know people who lived there and they were not dissatisfied. To my understanding, everyone got what was their 1st priotity, but there also is some chance that you cant get a dorm room.  Mixed reviews of Mejirodai, it was more expensive and did not seem as social, but new and nice. People would get pre-drinks at komaba all the time, also people from Mejirodai would go. I think Komaba Main was the easiest place to meet new people, I could just to my kitchen and join a group of people for drinks if I wanted to.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Shared kitchen for 36 people(or around that). Probably 4 people could cook at the same time. I didnt use the kitchen because its only slightly cheaper than eating out, and I went to Japan to have nice Japanese food not to cook myself which I can do back home

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: What I said above. Other options are sharehouse or finding an apartment. Dorms are probably the cheapest option of all, I paid 2.6k DKK (plus a little extras, maybe 3k total) a month with own bathroom, and I could walk home from Shibuya if I was out late. Sharehouse would be second best option probably, but I think many of them are not that social, and they might also not be students. So a bit risky. Own apartment will be more expensive. It can actually be quite cheap, but you have to rent for 2 years then. I heard there also was a craigslist-ish site where you can find apartments. If you want to research apartments, you have to be pretty good at googleing because eevrything is in Japanese.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I was studying at Hongo campus. Its a 45 min commute to get there. Even though you have to switch trains twice, its actually quite easy, with the train being right next to each other. If you can go there 3 times a week or less, its not really an issue. Taking the trip 4-5 times a week might be too much in the long run.
If you are undergrad you should 100% stay at komaba. If I went again, I would also still choose Komaba Main.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: From home there is a course catalog you can browse, which is quite easy to use. If you are a graduate(master), remember to use the graduate catalog. When you arrive, they will also explain at the orientation. Then, you have two weeks to 'shop' courses, where you can show up to any course. Next, you will have to finally choose the courses you want. The first week is normally not important, so skipping this is fine, if two courses are at the same time. The second week they start to go through important material, so it would be good not skipping this. You need 6 courses at economics. So you can maybe go to 8-10 the first week, then go to 7-8 second week if you are still unsure.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always go to the economics office. They are very helpfull, responds emails within one day, and there are people speaking English.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I had mixed experiences. You can get any course you want, its not like in some US uni where they fill up. The course registration itself is good, and easy to understand. You dont have to get permission from professors and other stuff like that, therefore 5/5. But I had two problems. First, I tried to registrer for two seminars, where you just had to listen to researchers present their papers. It was a little bit to ensure low workload for myself, but it was actually also good for me in relation to my thesis. Then in the middle of week two, I was told I could not register for them. So then I basically had to register two courses without the 'shopping' opportunity. It said nowhere I couldnt go to them, so I had no way of knowing.
Second, when I had to register for the new courses with short notice, I chose one course that was a quarter course (half semester, but still 2 credits). Therefore I completed that course after 2 months, and had 5 courses to still complete. However, you need to have 6 credits in each quarter(term). I basically had 7 in the first, then 5 in the second. Then I was told (also at the end of the shopping week, in 2nd term) I had to register for a 7th course. It did say this in one sentence in the prerequisite paper I read 3-5 months prior, but I just understood it as I needed 12 credits total. It also doent make any logical sense, but the Japanese really stick to the rules. Since I also had problems with the two seminars, and someone confirming my courses were fine, I dont get why I wasnt told this.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you are in doubt about your courses, or maybe just in general, ask the office about your registration and get it confirmed. They have a person who will look through all your courses and tell you (late) if something is wrong. I think the registration itself is 5/5 and very easy, I guess I was just unfortunate. If I had to do it again, I would ask the office to confirm all my courses, and confirm I didnt have to register more for the whole exchange.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Level depends. You can also registrer 2/6 courses at other departments. I did 3 (because of the extra one) at public policy (statskundskab), which was much easier than economics. Some economics courses were easy, but you still had to do some assignments. Some were quite hard. I did a data science course where I coulndt (and didnt really want to waste my time) hand in two huge assignments cause they were so difficult. Workload per cource is also less than KU, but you have more courses. I had a lot of assignments the last month/2 weeks. This was quite intense, but rest of semester was overall chill.
Workload public policy - 2*10 pages paper or 10 page paper and 5 min presentation. 
Workload economics - read 3 papers and write a summary/discussion + 3 econometric assignments with 5-10 questions (little long, quite easy though)+ 10 page research proposal or 8x15 min quiz + 3 home assignmens with 10 questions and read 2 papers.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Not similar at all. Most courses are around 10 ppl, so there is room for discussion. Its almost like a TA session at KU. Grading is also very different between courses. Some will be +50% class participation. Some will be presentation based, some test and some assignments. I mostly had assignment based grading, by choice, because I didnt want to read a ton of material and discuss. 
It is very easy to pass courses, and also relatively easy getting a good grade. I got several A's without much effort.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- International Trade I (pretty good course)
- Data Science for Practical Economic Research (Very difficult. Should be called "Computational theoretical econometrics modelling". There is NO data in this course)
- Institutional Analysis of Japanese Economy I (More of a history class in Japanese economy in samurai times) 
- Policy and Governance in Contemporary China (Public policy. Quite good, would recommend)
- Science and Technology in International Relations (Public policy. Very easy, didnt learn much)
- Labor Economics I (Good refresher for econometrics, quite easy)
- Energy Systems (Engineering/public policy. Fun/different and easy if you had physics A in highschool)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
International Trade, P&G in China, Labor economics. 
All relatively fair workload, and interesting topics
Some people did a Japanese class, didnt hear good things about it, but thats what the shopping week is for

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything is not as expensive as people think. I would say overall its around 2/3 Danish prices, maybe less. housing 3k, eating out is around 50-75DKK. Often drinks 40 DKK at a bar/club. You can probably be completely fine on your SU, if you can live on a budget. If you can get grants you should be covered.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Didnt really participate much in them. As said above I would like the orientation to be more social.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: In Japan they ahve a lot of clubs. They have them for almost anything to my understanding. There are both clubs and 'circles'. I think cirles are the less serious one. Normally exchange students cant join the real clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Some of my friends joined the less serious football club, which they liked and its a good place to meet new people. Just try to find them on the internet or instragram(just send them a DM). I think there were 4+ not serious football clubs. The serious ones train 5 times a week or something.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Probably visit Okinawa, Osaka, Kyoto or other places in Japan, many people went there. Often you can join a group of exchange students. It also takes more than 4 months to explore all of Tokyo, so you can also just stay in the city.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it was fine, but some people might get a bit of a culture shock. Japan is very different from Denmark, but it is clean, safe and organised. So you will feel that its different, but probably not in a bad way.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a sport club is probably the easiest. There was not that many Japanese ppl in the English courses, and I don't see how someone would casually get to know them in that setting. As all other people, Japanese are more open to talk over a beer/at bars, so thats maybe also an option. There also was some language exchange events, didnt go to them though

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Language is the biggest one. Get google translate downloaded, and use the camera function for text.
Don't speak extremely loud in the train, noone talks there.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Probably politeness and how clean and nice. And the food. Overall Japan is a very nice country to live in

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Get your paperwork done early and keep a good overview
2. If you go alone, try to make some friends at the dorm/orientation early on, and be a bit proactive to meet people. I think maybe could be a bit difficult to meet new people a month into the exchange.
3. Pro tip: in the iPhone wallet, you can create a suica/passmo card. Do it once you arrive. You can transfer money directly on your phone. The card works as a credit card in 90% of Japanese stores. Normally you have to get the card in a machine, ant add money with cash. 10x easier to get it in the wallet.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Maybe be strategic with your course selection in relation to what you want to get out of your exchange. I think its pretty easy to see if a course will be hard or easy. If you want to travel and explore, try to get some courses on the same days, with lower workload, then yoy can have a lot of freetime. If you want to go for the academics, I think many interesting academic courses with high worload was also offered. If you want, you can have courses where you get to discuss directly with the professor every class.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I think just the overall day to day lifestyle. I was living in Shibuya, I could go out to eat good food every day, I had some good friends to explore with and Tokyo is just very cool overall

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
(1) Language in combination with food. If you want to explore japanese restaurants, you will end up in a situation where noone speaks english, and the menu is hand written so goole cant translate it. Plus, many restaurants serve some weird stuff like intestines. If you are picky with your food, you probably want to make sure they have a translatable menu. But often these restaurants are very very good.
(2) Yakitori is not like in 7-11 in Denmark. If you order a mixed platter, half of them will be with stuff like chicken liver, - skin, or some meat you cant chew. So be aware

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
